1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6.name: Sicilian Defence: Old Sicilian
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6.background: One of Black's three main replies to 2.Nf3, with 2...d6 and 2...e6. Lines beginning 2...Nc6 that do not transpose into lines of 2...d6 have their own ECO codes, B30–B39; the most important among them are the Rossolimo, Kalashnikov, Sveshnikov and Accelerated Dragon.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4.strategy: The principled move: White trades the d-pawn for Black's c-pawn to open lines for every piece. Black keeps a d- and an e-pawn against White's single central pawn, White gets open lines for every piece, and the game turns open and sharp.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4.name: Sicilian Defence: Open

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5.strategy: Attacks the knight that guards d4 and e5, with the aim of taking it and doubling Black's pawns. White accepts giving up the bishop for the knight and avoids the heavy theory of the open Sicilian, playing instead for a structural edge in a slower, strategic game.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5.name: Sicilian Defence: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5.background: Its earliest recorded game is Bird against Horwitz in 1851. The Nyezhmetdinov–Rossolimo Attack is named for Nicolas Rossolimo, who first played it in 1948, and Rashid Nezhmetdinov, who played it in 1956. It is very popular at the highest levels: Fabiano Caruana played it in games 1, 3 and 5 of the World Championship match against Magnus Carlsen.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight and waits, leaving the choice between opening the centre and a slower, closed set-up for later. The price of that flexibility is that Black can occupy e5 with a pawn, which makes d4 hard to play and leaves White with a quiet game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to deflect Black's c-pawn and build a big centre at once, with the semi-open b-file and quick development as compensation. A whole pawn is a high price for that, so Black can accept it calmly.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.b4.name: Sicilian Defence: Portsmouth Gambit

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto: the bishop on g7 will help control the centre and make it harder for White to build a pawn centre, and the king gets a safe home. Black accepts the threat of doubled pawns for a solid game, with counterplay on the queenside or from the d4 outpost.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nb8.strategy: Undoes 2...Nc6 for nothing: Black has lost two tempi, and White's knight and bishop are developed while Black's army is still at home. The bishop on b5 achieves little, but White can take the centre at once and without risk.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nb8.name: Sicilian Defence: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Brooklyn Retreat Defence

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Na5.strategy: Sidesteps the bishop and avoids doubled pawns, but puts the knight on the rim, where it no longer guards d4 and e5 and can be harassed by the b-pawn. White gets a free hand in the centre against a badly placed piece.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4.strategy: Takes the pawn and removes White's d-pawn from the centre in return for Black's c-pawn: Black trades a wing pawn for a central one. After White recaptures, Black has two centre pawns against one, and the fight is about who profits from that.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 e6.strategy: Aims at control of d5, but cannot stop White from advancing there at once: the pawn attacks the knight and drives it away, gaining space with tempo. Black's pieces end up pushed back.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 e6.name: Sicilian Defence: Franco-Sicilian Variation

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5.strategy: Plants a pawn on e5 that guards d4, so White can no longer open the game with d4. Black gets space in the centre but leaves d5 as a hole, since neither the c5 nor the e5 pawn can cover it, and the game turns into a slow manoeuvring fight.
